text: This lab assembles the last four lessons into one orchestration design for a realistic scenario: a hundred fifty-iteration VQE loop that has to survive real-world queue congestion and occasional device failures without silently corrupting results or blowing a budget.

Eight parameters, seventeen evaluations per iteration, batched into one program-set submission, running on Rigetti Ankaa-3. Across the run, ten iterations hit a device-offline failure and recover on retry. Two of those exhaust their retry budget entirely and fall back to a flagged classical-simulator result.
Here's that real device — Rigetti Ankaa-3, as it actually appears on Amazon Braket. Step one of every iteration is checking exactly this status before submitting anything.

Now the arithmetic for a bad day. A normal iteration costs twenty dollars and forty cents. Ten iterations that fail once before succeeding on retry waste two hundred four dollars. Total run cost: three thousand two hundred sixty-four dollars. Without logging that two hundred four dollars as its own line item, a post-run cost review just sees the total — with no way to see that six point two five percent of it came from device failures, not from the optimization itself.
This is what the operational log actually has to capture, down to the field — device, status, cost, latency, every single iteration, visible on a real task detail page like this one.

And this is the real budget control all of it gets checked against — Amazon Braket's spending limits. Without this kind of per-QPU cap, a bad day like the one we just computed could keep compounding with nobody noticing until the invoice arrives.
That closes out orchestration. Chapter 4 turns to real, current provider pricing — so you can estimate a workload's cost before committing to an architecture, not after.
